issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (the stock inventory) and instruct students to modify/use it, but the template repository provides an 'Inventory' class that implements the expected stock behavior while the Stock.java file is empty. The solution also uses the Inventory class (SealSaloon defines a static Inventory stock). This name/file mismatch (Stock vs Inventory, plus an empty Stock.java) is a structural inconsistency that will confuse students about which class to modify/use and where to implement the required methods.
issues.suggested_fix:
Make the naming consistent across problem statement, template, and solution. Either:
1) Rename the Inventory class/file to Stock in the template and solution (move/rename Inventory.java -> Stock.java and update references), and remove or populate the currently-empty Stock.java file; OR
2) Update the problem statement and UML to use the name 'Inventory' everywhere instead of 'Stock', and remove the empty Stock.java file from the template. Ensure SealSaloon and all instructions consistently refer to the same class name so students know which file to edit/use.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (and describe its methods), but the template and solution code provide a class named 'Inventory' that implements the described stock functionality. This mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) creates a mapping barrier: students reading the problem will look for/expect a Stock class and Stock-typed attributes/methods, but the starter code and reference solution expose these members via Inventory. It may confuse students about where to implement or call the Stock-related methods and which type to use for the shared stock attribute.
issues.suggested_fix: Align the identifier across artifacts. Either (A) update the problem statement and UML to refer to 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock' so it matches the provided code, or (B) rename the 'Inventory' class (and its file) in the template and solution to 'Stock' (and update usages such as the SealSaloon.stock declaration) so the code matches the problem. Option B keeps the wording in the spec and reduces student confusion when the statement mentions 'Stock'.
